They'd work through them in order until something gave. The group filed out into the hallway, Orela's flashlight leading. Somewhere in the dark behind them, just outside the beam's reach, a shape kept pace. Danny tucked his phone into his sleeve and melted backward into the dark, footsteps silent despite the water — it had climbed past his ankles while he wasn't paying attention, which was mildly annoying, and his robes dragged through it with the heavy, sodden pull of fabric that had given up trying to stay dry. The long straps floated around him, trailing dark patterns across the surface. He'd have to do something about the mold smell later. The leather was going to hold it for weeks if he didn't treat it properly, and the canvas underlayer was probably already past saving if he was being honest with himself. Later problem. Right now, the beam of Orela's flashlight was painting the group in sharp relief — five people, wet and tired and moving with the grim purpose of survivors who had run out of other options — and he had a camera, a clear angle, and absolutely no intention of missing a single moment of what came next. He adjusted his position, keeping to the dark at the edge of the beam, and watched the rats work the maze. Ch 5 – Under Pressure The water lapped around their ankles with gentle, steady persistence. The hallway stretched longer than it had any right to as the group worked their way through, five shadows in single file, led only by the beam of Orela’s flashlight. The air hung heavy around them, thick with dampness and the sour rot of slow decay, clinging damp and thick to the inside of their throats. It felt unnatural. Processed. Rancid. Recycled through old pipes and bleeding walls. Every breath felt humid. Every movement whispered. The floor felt soft in places, like the linoleum had given up beneath the rising tide. The creeping flood found their calves before they'd made it halfway down the hall. Nobody announced it. Nobody needed to. It was just suddenly there, cool and present against skin that had almost — almost — dried out in the classroom, and the group absorbed the information in their own individual silences. Here we go again. That was the sum total of what Dwight's nervous system had to say about the situation, delivered with the flat certainty of something that had already been through this once tonight and had not enjoyed it. He kept his eyes forward and his breathing measured and his hands away from the walls because touching the walls meant feeling how damp they were, and feeling how damp they were meant thinking about where that moisture was coming from, and that was a thought he wasn't ready to finish. His footsteps stuttered through the water. Not enough to call attention, but enough to tell. His gaze kept flicking between the others, fingers twitching at his side. Five. That number had been pinging something at the back of his brain since Jake said it aloud. Five survivors. Five people. One too many. There was never supposed to be five. He couldn’t explain it, didn’t have the words for what it meant, but he felt it under his skin like a splinter. The Entity’s work was always symmetrical. Ritualistic. Four survivors. Four ways back to the campfire. Two exits. Balance was how the Fog functioned. Five was off. Five was bait. He didn’t see the water creeping higher anymore. Didn’t see the shadows moving differently. He saw numbers. Patterns. Ratios. He was spiraling inward like a whirlpool, understanding just barely out of reach. David limped alongside Dwight — jaw set, shoulders square, vision narrowed down to the hallway’s vanishing point. He was trying not to cough, breath kept shallow as he focused on the next few steps. If he kept his focus locked on the exit and ignored the pull of the water around his calves, maybe he wouldn’t feel how soft his knees had gotten. He desperately needed to rest. He could feel it behind his eyes, but he shelved it. Later. He could fold later. Once they were out. Leon kept his eyes on the middle distance. Not the floor. Definitely not the floor. Dwight’s warning about the water rising faster than natural echoed in his head like a drip. Ribs in minutes. Ceiling in under half an hour. He knew what that kind of pressure felt like, lungs too tight, world flipping upside down. He'd looked at the floor once, briefly, when the water was still just a shimmer across the tile back in the classroom, and something in the back of his brain had pulled up a memory he hadn't asked for — dark lake water, the specific pressure of something large moving beneath him — and he'd slammed the door on it before it could finish the sentence. He was fine. The hallway was flooded, not a lake. Completely different. He kept his eyes up. The memory knocked again, politely, and he ignored it. Jake hadn't stopped glaring at the walls since they left the classroom. Not the water, not the ceiling, not the general wrongness of the hallway — the walls specifically, like he was waiting to catch them doing something. His grip on the crowbar hadn't loosened since they'd left the classroom. “This whole building's rotting from the inside out, Entity’s in the fuckin’ plumbing,” he muttered. “Watch your backs. Wouldn’t be surprised if Her creepy-ass bug legs burst out of the floor next.” “Maybe don’t tempt her, huh?” Orela muttered softly, sweeping her light nervously around the edges where the water met the walls.
